clue.text: This is on hand to provide quick coverage?

definitions.text: This is on hand to provide quick coverage?

parts.words: on hand to provide quick coverage
parts.note: surface reading: someone standing by, ready to stand in at short notice
setter's reading: the quick is the tender flesh at a fingertip, and this thing grows on the hand over it

explanation.surface: A reserve worker always available to cover a shift at short notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On hand' sounds like 'available' and 'quick' like 'fast'; read literally, it sits on the hand and covers the quick, the sensitive skin at the end of each finger.
explanation.definitionFit: The horny plate at each fingertip literally shields the sensitive flesh called the quick.

parts.note: slang: both mean excellent or terrific

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A wicked, extremely convoluted tale, the kind told by a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' looks like evil, but here it is the slang of approval, as in 'that's wicked!', matching FAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A fable is a short tale, often with animals and a moral, so it is a kind of narrative.

clue.text: Munch for instance on grain we cooked

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients into something new, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone munching on a bowl of cooked grain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Munch' looks like a verb about eating, but with a capital M it is Edvard Munch, painter of The Scream.
explanation.definitionFit: Edvard Munch was born in Norway, so he is an example of a person from that country.

indicators.note: losing the head means losing the top, so the opening letter is cut off

parts.note: standard abbreviation
a monarch rules a country

explanation.surface: An English king executed, apparently by a scheming Swiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calculating' looks like 'scheming', but it means doing mathematics: Leonhard Euler was the great 18th-century Swiss mathematician.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler, born in Basel, was among history's most prolific mathematicians, hence a Swiss man who computes.

clue.text: South leaving card game for sleep

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: a children's card game where players shout when matching cards appear
compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone from the south quitting a card game to go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: SNAP is a children's card game; take away the S and a short sleep is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A nap is a brief doze, usually during the daytime, so it is a short spell of slumber.

parts.note: surface reading: a person whose nature is to get visibly anxious
setter's reading: sloping print, used to emphasise a word

explanation.surface: A personality that tends to look tense and anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' is a kind of person and 'stress' is anxiety in the surface; really, type is printed lettering, inclined means slanted, and stress is emphasis on a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Slanted printing lettering is the usual typographic means of marking emphasis in text.

indicators.note: to keep is to hold onto, so one piece holds another inside it

parts.note: a partner's son from a previous relationship
a hen is a domestic fowl

explanation.surface: An engineer's relative who keeps chickens.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking definition to wordplay. George Stephenson was the English railway engineer who built the Rocket locomotive.
explanation.definitionFit: George Stephenson and his son Robert were pioneering British railway builders, famous for steam locomotives.

clue.text: Wood losing mass in Roman river

indicators.note: whatever is lost is no longer there, so that letter drops out

parts.note: timber is wood used for building
M is the symbol for mass

explanation.surface: A log floating in a river in Rome and gradually losing weight.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the standard physics symbol for mass; removing it from TIMBER leaves the river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tiber is the river flowing through the city of Rome into the Tyrrhenian Sea.

clue.text: Boy harbours plot in Finnish parts

indicators.note: a harbour shelters ships within it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a lad is a boy
a plot is a scheme or plan

explanation.surface: A boy secretly nursing a scheme while in Finland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' could be a patch of land, which fits Finnish parts, but here it is a scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapland is the northern region of Finland and neighbouring countries, home of the Sami people.

indicators.note: processing changes raw material into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hindus are said to be able to make processed cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Processed cheese' reads as one phrase, but 'processed' belongs to the wordplay and 'cheese' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a strong blue-veined dairy product from Denmark, a named variety of fromage.

clue.text: Favoured official made mistake on piano

indicators.note: in this setter's usage one thing written on another follows it, so the piece named after this word goes first

parts.note: p is the musical marking for piano, softly
short for referee, a sports official
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A referee who is favoured by one side blunders while playing the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On piano' puts the official and the mistake after P, the musical abbreviation for soft playing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something preferred is liked better than the alternatives, chosen or given special treatment.

clue.text: Draw fleet out: vessels from Holland?

indicators.note: something out is disordered or put out of place, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naval order to draw the fleet out, with Dutch ships in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' and 'vessels' both suggest ships, but the vessels are pots and jugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Delftware is blue and white glazed pottery made in the Dutch town of Delft, including jugs and bowls.

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: end of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A Scotsman currently living in Moravia, part of the Czech Republic.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a common Scottish first name often stands for any Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian is the Scottish form of John, a typical first name for a man from Scotland.

parts.note: surface reading: a cricket spectator cursing the screen behind the bowler, 'blinking' being a mild oath
setter's reading: a flap that blinks and screens the eye from view

explanation.surface: An exasperated batsman cursing the sight-screen at a cricket ground.
explanation.walkthrough: A sight-screen is the white board behind the bowler that helps the batsman see the ball; 'blinking' is a mild British expletive, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The fold of skin that closes over the eye blinks and shuts out vision, screening the sight.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the largest species of penguin
second meaning: Beethoven's fifth piano concerto bears this nickname

explanation.walkthrough: Each word is a type of thing with the same name: a species of penguin and the nickname of Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 5.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antarctic bird species and the famous Beethoven piece share the same imperial title as their name.

parts.note: standard abbreviation
to lose is to be defeated

explanation.surface: A pundit concludes that the Conservative candidate is beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative, a party in Britain and Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: To close something is to bring it to an end, as in finishing a meeting or speech.

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: French for not, as in ne ... pas

explanation.surface: A fool in France who refuses to come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' tells you to translate 'not' into French, giving PAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sap is a gullible or foolish person, informal slang for a dupe or simpleton.

parts.note: night is the dark part of the day
a wood is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: A spooky, gloomy forest that might be haunted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haunt' looks like a verb for ghosts, but it is a noun: a place people frequent. A wood is a golf club with a large head.
explanation.definitionFit: A haunt is a favourite place one visits often, and a late-night dancing venue is a typical one.

clue.text: Some of these eggs raised birds

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters makes them read from bottom to top
taking only some of a phrase means part of its run of letters is lifted out

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A few of these eggs have been hatched and reared into birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' suggests rearing chicks, but in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Geese are large waterfowl, plural of goose, so they are a kind of feathered creature.

indicators.note: what is devoured ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: lard is pig fat
Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone eaten by a fat, greedy landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' looks like an adjective for the landowner, but it is a noun giving LARD. A laird is a Scottish estate owner.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland a laird is the owner of a large estate, the local equivalent of a lord of the manor.

indicators.note: something spoiled is ruined and its order wrecked, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tale ruined by someone who kept ranting while telling it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoiled' reads as ruining the story, but it tells you to rearrange 'a ranter'.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to recount events in order, giving an account of what happened.

parts.note: the usual abbreviation

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An AI chatbot that genuinely helped from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' takes just the first letter of 'did', added after the familiar abbreviation AI.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid as a verb means to assist or support someone, a direct synonym.

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so a piece is enclosed

parts.note: taken as written
an engine that dies fails
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A student fails at university and says farewell to studying.
explanation.walkthrough: DIE goes inside A plus U; 'fail' as in a battery or engine giving out.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is the French farewell, used in English to mean a final parting word.

indicators.note: training reshapes and drills something into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A military brigade he had drilled captured a strategic spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The military surface is apt: 'trained' reads as drilled troops, but it signals rearranging 'brigade he'd'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridgehead is a foothold taken in enemy territory, from which an army can advance further.
